title: Quantum sensing composite excitations in an anisotropic ferromagnet via a qubit
authors: Amey S. Rodge, Tarek Moussa, Akashdeep Kamra, Bashab Dey
abstract: Ordered magnets harbor intrinsically squeezed ground states and magnonic excitations characterized by entanglement between spins and nonclassical magnon number composition. A pathway to detecting the superpositions of noneigenmode magnon number states underlying these nonclassical magnetic ground states has recently been demonstrated by utilizing a qubit coupled to the magnon mode via a direct dispersive interaction. Here, we theoretically develop this qubit spectroscopy further delineating the capabilities and limitations of this qubit spectroscopy for sensing the quantum superpositions that underlie the excited states. We demonstrate that the spectroscopy lends itself naturally to unraveling the superpositions that underlie the various quantized squeezed-magnon number states. However, excited states comprising superpositions of multiple squeezed Fock states become increasingly hard due to the large number of possible transitions, and resulting peaks, in the qubit spectroscopy thereby requiring qubits with narrower linewidths. Along the same lines, we theoretically demonstrate the qubit spectroscopy of a low amplitude coherent squeezed-magnon state analyzing the tradeoff between frequency crowding due to multiple transitions and peak linewidths. Our work lays the groundwork and design equations for deploying high-quality qubits towards sensing the composite nature of spin excitations in magnetic systems.
summary: The paper theoretically establishes qubit spectroscopy as a powerful tool to probe the complex, nonclassical superpositions present in magnon excitations within anisotropic ferromagnets. By analyzing the resonant peaks in the qubit's response, researchers can map out the underlying quantum state structure of the magnons. However, the study highlights critical limitations regarding spectral resolution and thermal noise that must be overcome for practical implementation.
main_problem: The goal is to develop a theoretical protocol using qubit spectroscopy to detect and characterize quantum superpositions underlying nonclassical magnon excitations in anisotropic ferromagnets.
main_result: Qubit spectroscopy can successfully resolve these intrinsic magnonic superpositions, but the technique suffers from spectral crowding and poor resolution when probing highly complex or finite-temperature excited states.
method: The method involves coupling a superconducting qubit dispersively to the magnon mode and measuring the resulting shifts in the qubit's frequency as a function of the driving field.
model_or_system: The system is an anisotropic ferromagnet hosting magnons, modeled by a spin Hamiltonian leading to squeezed magnon excitations. The dynamics are analyzed using coupled quantum mechanical models involving the qubit and the bosonic magnon mode.
key_observables: Resonant peaks in the qubit spectrum ($\omega_{mn}$), whose heights are proportional to the squared overlap coefficients of the underlying magnon number state superpositions.
important_parameters: Magnon decay rate ($\kappa_m$), qubit decay rate ($\kappa_q$), and temperature ($T$).
main_assumptions: The protocol is fundamentally limited by spectral crowding when many transitions are close, and finite temperatures significantly degrade the measurement fidelity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the simulation of the qubit excitation spectrum as a function of driving frequency, showing multiple peaks corresponding to different magnon transition channels ($\omega_{mn}$), and demonstrating peak broadening/mismatch at non-zero temperature.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework for coupling the qubit to the squeezed magnons, derives the spectroscopic signatures from the resulting Hamiltonian, analyzes the feasibility of probing various superposition states, and concludes by detailing limitations related to spectral resolution and thermal effects.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum information concepts (qubit spectroscopy) with condensed matter physics (magnonics), providing a concrete theoretical roadmap for using superconducting qubits as highly sensitive probes for exotic many-body quantum states in magnetic materials.
